newsitem.title: USA: Screams of "fire" as ValuJet crashed in Everglades.
newsitem.headline: Screams of "fire" as ValuJet crashed in Everglades.

text.p: Frantic passengers screamed "fire" in the final moments of ValuJet Flight 592, and a series of critical errors led to the shipping of hazardous oxygen canisters in the cargo hold, according to documents released on Monday.

Hundreds of pages of documents were made public at the start of a National Transportation Safety Board (NSTB) hearing into the cause of the May 11 crash. The ValuJet DC-9 plunged into the Florida Everglades a few minutes after takeoff, killing all 110 people on board.
The documents included transcripts of recordings of conversation on the doomed jet's flight deck, shouts of "fire" from the passenger cabin and a cry for oxygen from a flight attendant.

Mechanics who handled the dozens of outdated oxygen generators suspected of starting or fueling a fierce fire on board the aircraft had been working long shifts, according to the documents. The workers may have been pressured into signing-off on work -- required to show that procedures have been followed -- in fear of their jobs, the reports indicated.

The oxygen generators had been removed from another ValuJet aircraft and stored before being placed on Flight 592 for transport to Atlanta. But the small metal cylinders were not properly labeled as hazardous material and did not have safety caps to prevent accidental activation, the documents said.
Instead, mechanics cut or taped lanyards to the sides of the canisters as an alternative method of rendering the canisters inoperative, the documents said.

One mechanic said he was "aware of the need for safety caps prior to the time he signed-off the (work) card," the documents stated. "He felt he had been given a mandatory order and that his job depended on compliance with it," the report said.

SabreTech Corp. president Steven Townes, the first witness at the week-long public hearing, said the two mechanics who loaded the canisters were no longer employed by SabreTech, one of the nation's largest aircraft maintenance contractors.
While refusing to concede that mistakes were made, Townes said "powerful" lessons had been learned in the aftermath of the crash.
He said federal regulations for the handling of hazardous material needed to be tightened.
"Not one of those oxygen canisters was labeled clearly as a hazardous material," Townes said. "My mechanics should not have to guess."
Townes skirted repeated questions about whether all employees at the company's Miami base were required to speak English and able to read repair manuals and instructions.

"To my knowledge there was no language issue in our operations," he said in answer to questions of whether SabreTech tested the English skills of all employees who worked on aircraft. NTSB investigators said there may have been a communications problem at the SabreTech facility.
Transcripts of conversations in the cockpit and noises aboard the DC-9 in its final moments clearly indicated the presence of fire in passenger cabin.
"Fire, fire, fire, fire," a female voice in the cabin said about six minutes into the flight. "We're on fire, we're on fire," a male voice echoed seconds later.
Seconds before, pilot Candi Kubeck was heard on the voice recorder talking about a suspected malfunction in the electrical system. "We're losing everything," Kubeck said.
In the next minute, a voice believed to be that of a flight attendant said "OK, we need oxygen, we can't get oxygen back there."
NTSB chief investigator Greg Feith said it was not yet known whether the fire had knocked out the emergency oxygen system. "I don't know what she was referring to," he said.

Dozens of family members of the crash victims sat in a reserved section in the cavernous meeting hall at a hotel near Miami International Airport. Some of them said they had not been impressed by what they heard.
"I think it's going to be a game of the little mouse looking toward the big cat and saying, you know, 'You were wrong'," said Laura Sawyer, 22, whose grandparents were killed in the crash.

"I think it's going to be everybody pointing fingers back and forth at one another saying 'oh, they were responsible and why weren't they watching'," she said. "I don't think anyone is going to take full responsibility."
